prompt: Which of these apps can run its whole pipeline without a Mac?

choices.text: A React Native app published on both stores
choices.why: Its iOS half needs a Mac or EAS.

choices.text: A Swift app with no external libraries
choices.why: Any iOS build needs Xcode, so macOS.
Right. Android builds run on Linux.

choices.text: None of them; every store upload needs macOS
choices.why: Uploading to Google Play needs no Mac.

prompt: How many Xcode Cloud compute hours a month does Apple's developer membership include, per Apple's page in October 2026?
Which of these save Mac minutes? Choose every one.

choices.text: Running the listing and privacy checks on Linux
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: Building iOS only on tags and the release branch
choices.why: Right.

choices.text: A time limit on the macOS job
choices.why: Right. A hung simulator bills until killed.

choices.text: Building iOS on every commit to every branch
choices.why: That is how Mac minutes are wasted.

prompt: In the lesson, the cache key stayed the same after `check.ts` changed. Why is that right?

choices.why: Right. The key follows the lockfile, not the code.

choices.text: Node ignores TypeScript files when hashing
choices.why: Only the files named are hashed; that is the point.

choices.text: The cache expires every hour anyway
choices.why: Time is not part of the key.

choices.text: Comments are not part of a file's contents
choices.why: They are; check.ts was simply not hashed.

prompt: After `npm uninstall dayjs`, the key went back to its first value. What property does that show?

choices.text: That npm keeps a history of lockfiles
choices.why: The key comes from the file as it is now.
Nothing was deleted; the key was computed.
The third key shows it was.
Right. The key is a function of the lockfile's contents.

prompt: Why must a cache never hold the upload keystore?

choices.why: They store whole folders, binaries included.
Right. Including some pull requests: a cached keystore is a published one.

choices.text: The key would change every run
choices.why: The problem is who reads it, not the key.
Signing twice is not the risk.

prompt: Why is the keystore stored as Base64 in the CI service?

choices.text: Base64 encrypts it, so nobody can read the key
choices.why: Base64 is an encoding, readable by anybody; the secret store encrypts.

choices.text: Secrets are text and a keystore is binary
choices.why: Right. Base64 turns the bytes into text.
It reads the .jks file the script writes.
Base64 makes it about a third larger.

prompt: What does the `trap 'rm -rf "$work"' EXIT` line in `ci-sign.sh` protect against?

choices.why: It does not check passwords.

choices.text: The secret appearing in the job's log as plain text
choices.why: Masking and no `set -x` do that.
Each job has its own temporary folder.
Right. On the runner, after a failure or a success: it runs however the script ends.

prompt: Tracing with `set ___` echoes every command with its variables expanded, so it must never be on in a step that holds a secret.
With Play App Signing, what does a leak of the pipeline's secrets cost the planner?

choices.why: Right. The pipeline holds only the upload key.

choices.text: The app, which must be republished under a new name
choices.why: That is the cost of losing the app signing key, which the pipeline never holds.
Base64 hides nothing.
A signing key holds no user data.

prompt: In the workflow, why do the `android` and `ios` jobs say `needs: checks`?

choices.text: To share the cache with the checks
choices.why: `needs` orders jobs; it does not share caches.

choices.text: GitHub requires it for macOS jobs
choices.why: It is the workflow's choice.

choices.text: So a red check builds, signs and uploads nothing
choices.why: Right. And it spends no Mac minutes.
They run once.

prompt: The workflow's schedule runs `expiry.ts` every morning even when nothing is released. Why?

choices.text: So it goes red a month before a release would fail
choices.why: Right. Lesson 2's warning, on a clock.
The hour is not the point; the month is.

choices.text: To keep the macOS runner warm
choices.why: The checks job runs on Linux.
Nothing requires it; it is a choice.

prompt: What does the lesson ask instead of `actions/checkout@v4` in a real workflow?

choices.why: A branch moves even more than a tag.

choices.text: A copy of the action inside the repository
choices.why: Possible, but not what the lesson asks.
Right, with the version in a comment beside it. A tag can be moved by whoever controls it.
Actions are fine when pinned.

prompt: Put the steps of `ci-sign.sh` in the order they run.
items: refuse to start if a secret is missing
make a temporary folder and arrange its removal

prompt: A colleague adds `set -x` to the signing step to debug a failure. What is the risk?

choices.text: None, since CI services mask every secret
choices.why: They mask the exact value; derived forms slip past.

choices.text: The trace prints the secret in a form the mask misses
choices.why: Right. Never trace a step that holds one.
Slower is the least of it.
It runs; that is the problem.

prompt: Which part of the release does the workflow leave to a person?

choices.why: The pipeline signs.
The checks job runs it.

choices.text: Uploading to the internal track and TestFlight
choices.why: Fastlane does that in each build job.
Right. Lesson 7.
